name: John Chrysostom

seo.title: John Chrysostom: the Golden Mouth, his real quotes and feast days
seo.description: Who John Chrysostom was, in plain words: the preacher who angered an empress, his exiles, his real quotes and the fake ones, and his feast days.

band.lede: The preacher known as Golden Mouth, who told the rich the poor had a claim on their money and died in exile.

who: John was a preacher at Antioch, and then archbishop of Constantinople. His sermons later earned him the name Chrysostom, “golden-mouthed”. He told the rich that the poor had a claim on their money. He angered the empress, was exiled twice, and died on a forced march. More of his writings survive than of any other Greek Father.

roles.name: Monk
roles.line: Four years with a hermit, two alone in a cave

roles.name: Exile
roles.line: Sent away in 404, died on the road in 407

lines: By the church at Antioch, he said
If ten rich men did as much, there would be no poor
To his closest friend, from exile

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 347, at Antioch in Syria, today **Antakya in Turkey**.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: In Antioch, raised by his widowed mother **Anthusa**. He studied rhetoric under **Libanius**, the most famous pagan orator of the day.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **14 September 407**, at a martyr's chapel near Comana in Pontus, in today's **northern Turkey**. He was about 60.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: Beside the martyr Basiliscus, at Comana. In 438 his body was brought to the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople. Some relics later went to St Peter's in Rome, and in 2004 Pope John Paul II gave some back.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Chrysostom**, “golden-mouthed”, a name first found in writing in 553. **Ioann Zlatoust** in Russian. One of the **Three Holy Hierarchs**.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Copts, and a **Doctor of the Church** to Catholics. Anglicans and Lutherans remember him too.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: **Preachers**, named by Pope Pius X. Britannica adds orators, education and people with epilepsy.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: In icons, a bishop with a short dark beard and a high forehead, holding a Gospel book. In the West, a Latin bishop in a mitre.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: More than any other Greek Father: about 600 sermons and commentaries, books such as **On the Priesthood**, and about 240 letters, nearly all from exile.

portrait.alt: A Greek icon: John Chrysostom in bishop's robes marked with red crosses; below, a sailing ship carries his relics, and at the bottom a walled town lies among trees
portrait.credit: St John Chrysostom, the widow's vineyard, and the transfer of his relic. Greek icon from Kimolos. Byzantine and Christian Museum, Athens. Public domain.
portrait.caption: A Greek icon from the island of Kimolos. Above, John in his bishop's robes. Below, a small ship carries his relics to Constantinople, and at the bottom lies Comana, where he died. Byzantine and Christian Museum, Athens. Public domain.

typeNote: Serious here means he took people and things to heart, not that he was gloomy. The test names him first among the saints of The Forge.

west.text: The **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod**. It was the **Catholic** feast too, from the 13th century until 1969, and it is his day in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**.
**Catholic** memorial since 1969. Also the **Church of England** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: The return of his body to Constantinople in 438. **Greek** and **Russian** churches, and the **OCA**.
The **Three Holy Hierarchs**, with Basil the Great and Gregory the Theologian. **Greek** and **Russian** churches, and the **OCA**.
The day of his death, kept beside the Feast of the Cross. The **Russian Church**.
The day of his death, moved from 14 September. **Greek** and **Russian** churches, and the **OCA**.

feasts.note: Why so many dates? He died on 14 September, the Feast of the Cross, so the Greek Church moved him to 13 November. The Russian Church keeps both days. Rome kept 27 January, the day his body came home, until 1969. Then it took 13 September, the day the Syrians keep. Churches on the old calendar keep each Orthodox date 13 days later. The **Coptic** Church keeps him on 17 Hator, in its own calendar.

traits.title: a temper he kept in check
traits.text: He knew he had a temper. In On the Priesthood his friend Basil protests that John is far from anger. John asks why he wants “to provoke the wild beast when he is tranquil”. His calm came, he said, “not by any innate virtue, but by my love of retirement”. A friend from his youth said he showed “a proneness to irritability, rather than to modesty”.

cite.text: On the Priesthood, Book 3; Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapter 3

traits.title: would not stop saying it
traits.text: He knew some of his sermons annoyed people, and he preached them anyway: “And I know that I am giving disgust to my hearers. But what must I do? For this I am set, and I shall not cease to say these things, whether anything comes of them or not.” A historian who admired him says he was “naturally disposed to reprehend the misconduct of others”.

cite.text: Homilies on First Corinthians, Homily 40; Sozomen, Church History, Book 8, chapter 3

traits.title: ate alone, gave to the poor
traits.text: As archbishop he cut the bishop's own spending and built hospitals, with doctors and cooks. He gave no dinner parties. “I admit that he used to eat alone,” says his friend Palladius. He drank no wine, and he counted money spent on feasting men of pleasure as sacrilege. His enemies made it a charge against him.

cite.text: Palladius, Dialogue, chapters 5 and 12; Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapter 4

traits.title: tender with a friend in trouble
traits.text: From exile he wrote long letters to lift his friend Olympias out of despair: “pray do not deceive me by saying that you have thrown off all despondency”. He begged her to see good doctors, and sent word of a medicine that had cured him.

traits.title: not above a trick
traits.text: His friend Basil wanted them to face being made bishops together. When the day came, John hid, and Basil was taken and ordained. Basil came to him in tears, and John laughed: “I laughed for joy, and, seizing his right hand, I forced a kiss on him”. He wrote On the Priesthood to defend it.

said.lede: Palladius, a bishop who stood by him, wrote his Life soon after he died. Socrates and Sozomen wrote their histories about a generation later. Not all of it is praise.

quotes.q: It would have been John, had not the Christians taken him from us.
quotes.who: Libanius, his pagan teacher, asked on his deathbed who should take his place. Sozomen tells the story.

quotes.q: In public teaching he was powerful in reforming the morals of his auditors; but in private conversation he was frequently thought haughty and assuming by those who did not know him.
This most distressing journey took three months; yet the saint among all these annoyances was always the same shining star.
Here is a formidable dead man, who frightens living men, and men in authority too, as bogies frighten children.
quotes.who: His enemies' own clergy, on John in exile, as Palladius tells it

moments.title: His mother's plea
moments.text: His mother was widowed at twenty and raised him alone. His pagan teacher Libanius heard her story and cried out, “Heavens! what women there are amongst the Christians.” When his friend Basil urged John to leave home and share a house with him, she took him into her room. She sat by him on the bed where she had given birth to him, and begged him in tears. “Do not plunge me into a second widowhood,” she said. “Wait for my death.” For the time being, he stayed.

cite.text: On the Priesthood, Book 1; Letter to a Young Widow

moments.title: Two years in a cave
moments.text: He went up into the hills to live with an old hermit named Syrus, and stayed four years. Then he lived alone in a cave for two years, hardly sleeping and never lying down. It wrecked his stomach, and the cold harmed his kidneys. He had to come back to the city. His biographer calls that the Saviour's providence, “for the good of the Church”.

moments.title: The statues
moments.text: Angry at new taxes, a crowd in Antioch pulled down the statues of the emperor Theodosius. The city waited in terror for his revenge. All through that Lent John preached to calm and warn his people. About twenty of those sermons survive. Then Bishop Flavian came back from the capital with the emperor's pardon.

cite.text: Homilies on the Statues; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: Taken by stealth
moments.text: The emperor's chamberlain Eutropius wanted John as archbishop of the capital. But the people of Antioch would probably have rioted rather than let him go. So the governor called him to a martyrs' shrine outside the city, put him in a carriage and sent him off under guard. He was consecrated on 26 February 398.

cite.text: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 5; Sozomen, Church History, Book 8, chapter 2

moments.title: A consul at the altar
moments.text: Eutropius had tried to end the right of churches to shelter people. Then he fell from power, and ran to the church himself. He clung to the altar while soldiers and people called for his death. The next day John preached over him: “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” Eutropius was spared that day. He was caught later, outside the church, and put to death.

cite.text: Homily 1 on Eutropius, with its introduction; Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapter 5

moments.title: Deposed twice
moments.text: Theophilus of Alexandria gathered bishops at an estate called The Oak. They deposed John for refusing to come before judges who were his open enemies. He was sent away, and called back within days after a disaster in the palace frightened the empress. Months later he spoke against noisy games at her new silver statue, and she took it personally. In 404 the emperor told him to leave his church. He sent back: “I have received this Church from God our Saviour, for the care of the salvation of the people, and I cannot desert it; if, then, this is your will—for the city is yours—thrust me out by force.”

cite.text: Palladius, Dialogue, chapters 8 and 9; Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapters 15 to 18; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: The long road
moments.text: He was sent to Cucusus, a lonely village in Armenia, raided by bandits. From there he wrote to friends everywhere, helped the needy and bought back captives. His enemies thought he still had too much influence. So they had him marched towards Pityus, on the far shore of the Black Sea. He died on the way.

cite.text: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 11; Sozomen, Church History, Book 8, chapters 27 and 28

words.note: He left more writing than any other Greek Father. Most of these lines are from the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, translated in the 1880s.

feature.q: Would you do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked; do not while here you honor Him with silken garments, neglect Him perishing without of cold and nakedness.
feature.ctx: On how to honour Christ at the Eucharist. A little later he adds: “Do not therefore while adorning His house overlook your brother in distress, for he is more properly a temple than the other.”

quotes.q: Remember constantly that not to share our own riches with the poor is a robbery of the poor, and a depriving them of their livelihood; and that that which we possess is not only our own, but also theirs.
quotes.who: His best-known line on wealth, in F. Allen's translation of 1869. The Greek is stronger at the end: what we hold is not ours, but theirs. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it.

cite.text: Sermons on Lazarus and the Rich Man, Sermon 2

quotes.q: Why, this is what has ruined all, your supposing that the reading of the divine Scriptures appertains to those only, when you need it much more than they.
quotes.who: To people who said reading the Bible was for monks.

quotes.q: You both have become one man, one living creature; and do you still say my own? Cursed and abominable word that it is, it was brought in by the devil.
quotes.who: To a wife who said her money was still her own.

quotes.q: Tempers are wanted, not talking; character, not cleverness; deeds, not words.
quotes.who: On raising children: aim for character, not a clever speaker.

quotes.q: Attempt, sir, no such promise, nor order what is holy to be given to the dogs. I will never suffer the worshippers and praisers of the Divine Word to be expelled and their church to be given to them that blaspheme Him.
quotes.who: To the emperor Arcadius, who wanted to give a church to Gainas, a feared Arian general. As Theodoret reports it.

extras.title: Signs, as the historians tell them
extras.lede: The early sources credit him with no healings. They tell of signs around him instead, and the historians say plainly what they could not know.

items.title: The earthquake
items.text: The night after he was first sent away, says Theodoret, a great earthquake shook the city and terrified the empress. At daybreak envoys went to beg him back, and the people filled the strait with boats and torches to bring him home. Palladius speaks only of a disaster in the palace.
items.quote: In the night there was a great earthquake and the empress was struck with terror.

items.title: The fire
items.text: As he was led away for the last time, a flame broke out from his bishop's throne. It burned the great church, passed over the crowd in the street, and caught the Senate house. Palladius saw the hand of God in it. The fire spared the small building that held the church's treasures, he notes, so no one could say John had stolen them.
items.quote: This clearly showed that the marvel was heaven-sent

items.title: Hail, and the empress
items.text: On 30 September 404, hailstones of huge size fell on the city. Four days later the empress Eudoxia died. Bishop Cyrinus, one of John's loudest accusers, had already lost both feet after another bishop trod on one by accident. Many took it all as a judgment.
items.quote: These occurrences were by many regarded as indications of Divine wrath on account of the persecution that had been carried on against John.

cite.text: Sozomen, Church History, Book 8, chapter 27; Socrates, Book 6, chapter 19

items.title: The martyr in the night
items.text: On the last night of his march they lodged at the chapel of Basiliscus, a bishop of Comana who died a martyr. That night, says Palladius, the martyr stood by John and spoke to him. John took it as a sure warning. He died there the next day.
items.quote: Be of good cheer, brother; to-morrow we shall be together.

items.title: Doubted from the start
items.text: The historians say what they could not know. Socrates ends his account of the hail: “God only knows, Who is the discerner of secrets, and the just judge of truth itself. I have simply recorded the reports which were current at that time.” On the fire, he writes that “some of the Johannites set fire to the church”. Sozomen says each side blamed the other.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapters 18 and 19; Sozomen, Book 8, chapter 22

extras.title: The hard parts
extras.lede: Some of what he said and did is hard to read today. Here it is plainly, in his words and in his critics'.

items.title: Sermons against the Jews
items.text: At Antioch, about 387, he preached eight sermons usually called Against the Jews. They attack Judaism and the Jews of his day in the harshest terms. In the first he calls on the prophet Jeremiah, and says of the synagogue, in our translation from the Greek: *Where a prostitute stands, that place is a brothel. Or rather, the synagogue is not only a brothel and a theatre. It is also a den of robbers and a lair of wild beasts.*

cite.text: Against the Jews, Homily 1, in Greek. Our translation

items.title: Whom he was aiming at
items.text: He says whom he means: members of his own church drawn to the synagogue. In our translation: *Many of those ranked with us, who say they think as we do, go to watch the feasts. Others even keep the feasts with them and share their fasts. It is this evil habit I want to drive out of the Church now.* The scholarly English translation, by Paul W. Harkins (1979), is titled Discourses against Judaizing Christians.

cite.text: Against the Jews, Homily 1, in Greek. Our translation; Roger Pearse

items.title: What his critics say
items.text: Britannica says he spoke “with a degree of vitriol and abhorrence against Jews that was unusual even among his peers”. It gives both sides in one line: “Although some scholars assert that it is anachronistic to apply a modern understanding of antisemitism to a figure from the 4th century, his language is certainly hateful and unambiguous.” In our own time antisemites have posted the sermons online “as a justification for current anti-Semitism”, as Paul Halsall of Fordham University found.

cite.text: Britannica; Roger Pearse, quoting Paul Halsall

items.title: Temples torn down
items.text: As archbishop he sent bands of monks, armed with orders from the emperor, to pull down the pagan temples still standing in Phoenicia. He paid the workmen with gifts from rich Christian women, not with public money. Theodoret tells it as praise.
items.quote: John got together certain monks who were fired with divine zeal, armed them with imperial edicts and dispatched them against the idols' shrines.

items.title: Slavery
items.text: He said slavery came into the world as “the penalty of sin”, and that when Christ came, “He put an end also to this”. Yet he let a household keep one slave, or two at most. If the rich bought more out of kindness, he said, they should teach them a trade and set them free.
items.quote: when you have purchased them and have taught them trades whereby to support themselves, let them go free.

myths.claim: *He who is not angry when he has cause, sins.*
myths.truth: Not his. It comes from the Opus Imperfectum, a commentary on Matthew written by an Arian in the fifth century and long printed with his works. Aquinas quotes it as his. New Advent's edition of the Summa marks it “falsely ascribed to St. John Chrysostom”.

cite.text: Summa Theologiae, Part II-II, question 158; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.claim: *If you cannot find Christ in the beggar at the church door, you will not find Him in the chalice.*
myths.truth: These words are not in his sermons as translated in the 1880s. The idea is his, in Homily 50 on Matthew, quoted above: “Neglect Him not when naked”.

myths.claim: *The road to hell is paved with the skulls of priests.*
myths.truth: No such line is in his sermons as translated in the 1880s. What he did say is milder: “I do not think there are many among Bishops that will be saved, but many more that perish”.

myths.claim: He began a sermon against the empress: *Again Herodias raves; again she is troubled; she dances again.*
myths.truth: Socrates and Sozomen report that he did. But the sermon that survives with those words is not thought to be his. Schaff calls it “unworthy of his pen”. He thinks John probably said something about the empress that his enemies could read that way.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapter 18; Schaff, 1889

myths.claim: He wrote the Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom.
myths.truth: The Liturgy most used in Orthodox churches bears his name, but how much of it is his is disputed. The OCA says he “compiled a Liturgy”. The Catholic Encyclopedia says he “perhaps modified, but did not compose the ancient text”. Britannica calls the evidence unconvincing. The Prayer of St Chrysostom in the Book of Common Prayer comes from this Liturgy, “hence the attribution of the prayer”.

myths.claim: He studied at Athens with his friend St Basil the Great.
myths.truth: His friend Basil was a different Basil. Basil the Great was eighteen years older. Socrates took the two for one man. Some Greek and Coptic lives today send John to school at Athens beside Basil. The early accounts put his schooling at Antioch, under Libanius.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapter 3, with the NPNF note

myths.claim: After a sin with an emperor's daughter, he wandered in the wilderness as a penitent.
myths.truth: A later legend, engraved by Dürer and by Cranach. None of the early accounts tell it: not Palladius, Socrates, Sozomen or Theodoret.

cite.text: Art Institute of Chicago, on Cranach's Penitence of Saint John Chrysostom

stood.lede: Each line is John’s own, from his sermons, letters and books.

body.work: A letter to Olympias, from exile

circle.name: Libanius
circle.text: The great pagan orator who taught him rhetoric. He admired John's mother, and on his deathbed named John as the heir he had lost.

circle.name: Meletius of Antioch
circle.text: The bishop who noticed the bright young man and kept him close. He baptised him, made him a reader, and later a deacon.

circle.name: Olympias
circle.text: A rich widow and deaconess of Constantinople, and his closest friend. Seventeen of his letters to her survive. After his fall she was put on trial and would not give way.

circle.name: John Cassian
circle.text: Ordained by John at Constantinople, and loyal to him all his life. He called him “a marvel of faith and purity”.

cite.text: Cassian, On the Incarnation of the Lord, Book 7, chapter 31

circle.name: Pope Innocent I
circle.text: Bishop of Rome. He tried to get John a fair hearing, and his envoys were sent home in disgrace. The West would not share communion with John's enemies until his name was added to the roll of departed bishops.

cite.text: Sozomen, Book 8, chapter 28; Theodoret, Book 5, chapter 34

circle.name: Theophilus of Alexandria
circle.text: He opposed making John bishop, but had to consecrate him. Five years later he led the Synod of the Oak that deposed him.

circle.name: The empress Eudoxia
circle.text: At first she backed him: she paid for the silver crosses carried in his night processions. Then she took his sermons against luxury as aimed at her, and pressed for both his exiles.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapters 8, 15 and 18

circle.name: Epiphanius of Salamis
circle.text: A bishop from Cyprus who came to the capital to condemn Origen's followers, and turned against John. They are said to have parted with barbed prophecies. Socrates adds: “I cannot be sure that those who reported these things to me spoke the truth”.

death.big: He died on the road into a harsher exile, on 14 September 407, at a martyr's chapel near Comana in Pontus.
paras: Soldiers marched him for three months towards Pityus, at the far edge of the empire. One guard was kind to him in secret. The other marched him through pouring rain and hot sun, hoping he would die.
Near Comana they spent the night at the chapel of the martyr Basiliscus. In the morning John begged them to wait. They set off anyway, but he fell so ill that they turned back.

At the chapel he asked for white clothes, and changed everything down to his shoes. He gave the rest away. He received Communion and prayed his usual words. At the last Amen he signed himself with the cross, and died.
He was buried beside Basiliscus. So many monks and virgins came from Syria, Cilicia, Pontus and Armenia that people thought they had been sent for.

later.title: A later story
later.text: Later accounts, told today by the OCA, say his coffin could not be moved until the emperor wrote to John asking forgiveness. They say the body was found whole, and that John opened his mouth in church and said “Peace be to all”. They say many sick were healed at his tomb. None of this is in Socrates or Theodoret, who both wrote while that emperor still reigned. Theodoret tells only that the emperor laid his head against the coffin and prayed for pardon for his parents.

cite.text: OCA, Translation of the relics of Saint John Chrysostom; Theodoret, Church History, Book 5, chapter 36

items.k: Leaving his church for the last time
items.q: I see that the things concerning me have an end; I have finished my course and perhaps you will see my face no more.
items.ctx: To Olympias and three other women of his church, in the baptistery. He is echoing Paul.

items.q: Glory to God for all things
items.ctx: His “customary formula”, says Palladius. Then he signed himself with the cross at the last Amen.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Copts count him a saint, and Anglicans and Lutherans remember him too.

churches.status: Saint and Doctor of the Church

churches.note: One of the Three Holy Hierarchs
On 17 Hator, in its own calendar
A Lesser Festival in the Church of England. Also the Episcopal Church

paras: He died deposed, and out of favour at court. The bishops of the West would not share communion with his enemies until his name was added to the roll of departed bishops. In 438 the emperor Theodosius the Younger, son of the empress who had exiled him, brought his body home. He laid his head against the coffin and prayed for pardon for his parents.

quotes.q: John the glory of the Episcopate of Constantinople, whose holy life obtained the reward of martyrdom without any show of Gentile persecution
quotes.who: John Cassian, whom he ordained, writing about 430

cite.text: Cassian, On the Incarnation of the Lord, Book 7, chapter 30

quotes.q: At Constantinople, St. John, bishop, who was surnamed Chrysostom, on account of his golden flow of eloquence. He greatly promoted the interests of the Christian religion by his preaching and exemplary life, and after many toils, closed his life in banishment.
quotes.who: The Roman Martyrology, 1916 edition, for 27 January

kin.name: Jerome
kin.text: The great translator of the Bible was a fighter by his own account. He wrote that in an argument he threw himself into the thick of it.

kin.name: Paul the Apostle
kin.text: When the church in Jerusalem was still afraid of Saul, Barnabas, the “Son of Encouragement”, brought him to the apostles. Later the two fell out over young Mark, who had once left them. Barnabas wanted to give him a second chance. Paul would not. “Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company.” John himself said of the two: “the one was more tender and indulgent, but this one more strict and austere”.
kin.cite: Acts 4:36; 9:27; 15:36-40; St John Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts

tidbits.text: Some people in his day called another bishop Chrysostom for his fine voice: Antiochus of Ptolemais. In 404 Antiochus was one of four bishops who pressed the emperor to drive John out.

cite.text: Sozomen, Church History, Book 8, chapter 10; Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 10

tidbits.text: Crowds at Constantinople pushed so hard to hear him that people were in danger. So he sat on the readers' platform, in among them, and taught from there.
Some parents in his day lit lamps, gave each a name, and picked the name of the one that burned longest, for a long life. He wanted children named after the saints instead.
